topic.name: Priority of operations
topic.description: Use conventional notation for the priority of operations including brackets, powers, roots, and reciprocals; apply BIDMAS/BODMAS consistently to evaluate complex numerical expressions
evidence: Evaluate expressions involving brackets, indices, and all four operations in the correct order
Explain why the order of operations is necessary to avoid ambiguity
Use the reciprocal of a number and understand that a number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} evaluate a complex expression like '5 + 2³ ÷ 4' correctly — applying the right order of operations, handling the power before the division and division before the addition?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: extend the order of operations to include POWERS, ROOTS and RECIPROCALS — use conventional priority notation (BIDMAS/BODMAS) to evaluate complex numerical expressions, and understand a number times its reciprocal is 1.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use conventional notation for priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.EE.1 (write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents); the precedence of exponents within order of operations is formalised in Grade 6.
• Operational details — insert the Indices/Orders tier between Brackets and ×÷: Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (L→R) → +− (L→R). Evaluate expressions like 3 + 2³ × 4 or √(9+16). Introduce the reciprocal (1/n) as the multiplicative inverse — n × 1/n = 1 — and note division by n equals multiplication by its reciprocal. Reinforce that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, extended, not a new rule set.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): evaluate an expression with one power correctly (3 + 2³×4 = 35). Tier B (11–12): evaluate an expression mixing brackets, a root/power and all four operations. Tier C (12): explain why order of operations avoids ambiguity, and use a reciprocal (n × 1/n = 1; ÷n = ×1/n).
bestPractices: Slot the new INDICES tier explicitly into the already-secured Y6 hierarchy (prerequisite mt_jHgRQ4hR0g): powers and roots sit just below brackets and above ×÷ — present it as an extension of a known ladder, not a fresh acronym.
Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share a tier and +− share a tier (swept L→R); the BIDMAS acronym still misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S, so rehearse counterexamples with powers added.
Teach the reciprocal via the defining property n × 1/n = 1 and connect ÷n = ×1/n — seeding fraction division and later algebra; use it to show why reciprocals are 'undo by multiply'.
Confront power-specific traps directly: 2³ means 2×2×2 = 8 (not 2×3 = 6), and −3² vs (−3)² differ because the power binds tighter than the negative sign unless bracketed.
Motivate with genuine ambiguity: show a calculator or two people disagreeing on 3 + 2³ × 4, then resolve with the extended hierarchy, so the convention is felt as necessary.
keyRepresentations: Extended hierarchy ladder with the new Indices step inserted between Brackets and ×÷.
Colour-tiered annotation of an expression (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before evaluation.
Reciprocal pairing: n and 1/n shown multiplying to 1 (e.g. on a number line or as a product returning to unity).
Step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line (3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35).
commonMisconceptions: Evaluating powers as multiplication: 2³ = 6 instead of 8.
Applying the acronym literally — doing division before multiplication or addition before subtraction because I/D/A appear first.
Mishandling sign vs power: −3² taken as (−3)² = 9 rather than −(3²) = −9.
Thinking the reciprocal of n is −n (confusing multiplicative inverse with additive inverse) rather than 1/n.
Treating roots as outside the hierarchy, or evaluating under a root before resolving the bracket-like grouping the root implies (√(9+16) ≠ √9 + √16).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend the order of operations to include an Indices tier (powers and roots) sitting between brackets and ×÷, and introduce the reciprocal as the multiplicative inverse (n × 1/n = 1, with ÷n = ×1/n). Learners evaluate complex expressions tier by tier, confront power-specific traps (2³ ≠ 2×3; −3² vs (−3)²; a root sign implies grouping), and grasp that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, not an arbitrary rule. Activities range from a live expression-resolving tool (primary proposal) through anchor charts, consolidation questions, and Socratic justification.

activities.title: Resolve the expression one tier at a time
feedback: If a learner gives 2³ = 6, write 2×2×2 and count the factors: the exponent says how many copies of the base are multiplied together, not what to multiply the base by.
If a learner evaluates √9 + √16 = 7, point to the grouping the root sign implies: resolve 9+16 = 25 first, then √25 = 5.

If a learner adds before multiplying (power resolved to 2³ = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44), replay both orders side by side so the diverging answers (44 vs 35) show why multiplication is resolved before addition; separately, if a learner misreads the power itself (e.g. 2³ read as 2×3 = 6), handle that as the power-meaning error above.

Optional live supports that make the mechanism concrete: a tier-highlighter that shades each band as it is resolved; a step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line; a tool that refuses the mis-ordered path and plays out both answers for comparison. These are illustrative, not required.
activities.rationale: Order of operations with an added tier is structural and sequential; resolving an expression step by step, including a deliberate wrong-order comparison, targets the common error of treating the acronym as a literal sequence and of mishandling powers and roots. KS3 names powers and roots within priority notation and Grade 6 formalises the precedence of exponents.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
Grade 6 pupils write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents, formalising the precedence of exponents within the order of operations.
learnerActions: Work with a live expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and decide which operation to resolve next, following the hierarchy Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (left to right) → +− (left to right).
Resolve the power first: 2³ = 8 (write out 2×2×2 to confirm it is not 2×3 = 6), then ×4 = 32, then +3 = 35.
Deliberately try the wrong order — doing the addition before the multiplication: 3 + 2³ = 11, then × 4 = 44 — and compare 44 with the correct 35 so the two answers are seen to diverge.
Annotate an expression by shading each tier a different colour (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before collapsing it one tier per line: 3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35.
Evaluate √(9+16): resolve the grouping under the root first (9+16 = 25) then take √25 = 5, and check that this is not √9 + √16 = 3+4 = 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Indices (powers and roots) rank just below brackets and above ×÷; evaluating in the agreed order produces one unambiguous value, and a root implies grouping of what sits under it.

activities.title: The sign-versus-power boundary: −3² vs (−3)²
feedback: If a learner says −3² = 9, show that the exponent attaches to the 3 only: −3² reads as the negative of 3², i.e. −(9) = −9.
If a learner treats (−3)² as −9, point out the bracket groups the minus with the 3 so both factors are negative, giving +9.
An optional toggle that drops a bracket in and shows the answer flip 9 ↔ −9 makes the boundary vivid; a fixed worked pair of both cases also teaches it.
activities.rationale: The −3² vs (−3)² confusion is a named misconception; making the bracket's effect explicit addresses it directly without claiming a single medium is required.
learnerActions: Evaluate −3² by noting the power binds tighter than the negative sign: −3² = −(3²) = −9.
Evaluate (−3)² where the bracket groups the negative with the base: (−3)² = (−3)×(−3) = 9.
Add or remove a bracket around a negative number and predict how the value flips between −9 and 9 before confirming.
activities.intendedInsight: Without brackets, a power applies only to the number immediately beneath it, not to a preceding minus sign; bracketing changes what the exponent acts on.

activities.title: Reciprocals as multiplicative inverse
feedback: If a learner says the reciprocal of n is −n, check the defining property: n × (−n) is not 1, but n × 1/n = 1.
If a learner cannot link reciprocals to division, show ÷n and ×1/n acting on the same number and compare the results.

An optional reciprocal station where a number is dragged onto its ×1/n partner and the product settles to 1, with a ÷n swapped for ×1/n to see them land identically, makes the inverse relationship observable; a number line showing n and 1/n multiplying to unity works similarly.
activities.rationale: Teaching the reciprocal via its defining property seeds fraction division and later algebra and counters the additive-vs-multiplicative inverse confusion. KS3 priority notation explicitly includes reciprocals.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
learnerActions: State the reciprocal of a non-zero number n as 1/n and multiply n × 1/n, confirming the product is exactly 1 (e.g. 5 × 1/5 = 1); note that 0 has no reciprocal.
Compare dividing by n with multiplying by 1/n on the same number, checking the two operations give the same result (÷n = ×1/n).
Distinguish the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse, 1/n) from the negative (additive inverse, −n): the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5, not −5.
Match each number to its reciprocal (e.g. 4 ↔ 1/4, 2/3 ↔ 3/2).
activities.intendedInsight: Any non-zero number times its reciprocal is 1, so the reciprocal is what you multiply by to 'undo' multiplication, and dividing by a non-zero number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (0 has no reciprocal).

activities.title: Why do we need an agreed order? (justify the convention)
feedback: If a learner says 'that's just the rule', show the same expression producing two answers under two orders and ask which one others should read it as.
Accept any explanation that captures the idea that shared notation must yield one value to be useful for communicating calculations.
activities.rationale: The conceptual heart of this topic is ambiguity-removal; a discussion or Socratic prompt supports justification, which procedural practice alone may leave implicit. This is complementary to the hands-on evaluation, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Take a single expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and compute it under two different orders, recording the two different values (e.g. 35 vs 44).
Explain in your own words why mathematicians need one agreed order: so the same written expression communicates a single unambiguous value.
Respond to a prompt that offers two conflicting values and justify which order and result is correct and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of operations exists to remove ambiguity so notation communicates one value, not because any single order is inherently 'more correct'.

activities.title: Consolidation check
feedback: For 3 + 2³ × 4, flag 44 as the 'added before multiplying' error (power resolved to 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44) and any value using 2³ = 6; confirm 35 with the tier order.
For √(9+16) + 2×5, check the learner resolved the grouping under the root (25 → 5) before combining with 2×5 = 10, giving 15.
activities.rationale: Short checks consolidate and surface residual errors (adding first, exponent-as-multiplier, sign/power). Recognition and matching test outcomes rather than building the structural insight, so use them after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3 + 2³ × 4 and justify why 35 is correct (not 44 from adding before multiplying, and not using 2³ = 6).
Decide whether −3² equals −9 or 9 and explain the bracket rule.
Resolve √(9+16) + 2×5 in correct priority.
Match numbers to their reciprocals and state what each pair multiplies to.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can evaluate expressions with the new tier correctly and articulate the reciprocal relationship under assessment conditions.

constraints: Present the Indices tier as an extension of the already-secured brackets→×÷→+− hierarchy, not a brand-new acronym.

Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share one tier and +− share one tier, both swept left to right; BIDMAS/BODMAS still misleads on division-before-multiplication and addition-before-subtraction even with indices added — rehearse counterexamples.
A root sign implies grouping of what sits beneath it: resolve under the root before taking the root (√(9+16) = √25 = 5, not √9 + √16 = 7).

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks assess outcomes but do not by themselves build the structural, step-by-step insight; pair them with activities where learners resolve expressions and witness the reciprocal returning to 1.

Optional interactive supports (tier-highlighter, wrong-path comparison, drag-to-reciprocal station) make mechanisms concrete but are illustrative examples, not required mechanisms; the same ideas can be taught on paper or with worked pairs.
A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated live but can still teach the −3² vs (−3)² and reciprocal relationships.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness is claimed.

The 44 value is the intended wrong-order result for 3 + 2³ × 4, reached by resolving the power first (2³=8) and then adding before multiplying (3+8=11, ×4=44). It demonstrates that multiplication precedes addition, and is used only as a flagged error, never as a correct option.

Audit of the original assessment: the diagnostic prompt 'Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4²' has correctAnswer 50 (4²=16, 3×16=48, 2+48=50) — arithmetically correct, and the probeDeeper question 'Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?' is consistent with it.

The assessment distractor '2 + (3×4)² = 146' is arithmetically correct ((12)²=144, +2=146) and is a valid wrong-order distractor; used conceptually in consolidation without presenting it as a correct answer.
The source claim that BIDMAS/BODMAS misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S is NCETM-attributed guidance (verified:false in the row); preserved in constraints but not cited as established efficacy.
The parentTitle 'Ratio (age 11+)' appears inconsistent with the order-of-operations/reciprocals content; flagged as a possible source mislabel, not resolved here.

probeDeeper: Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?
What would this expression equal if we just went left to right — and why is that not allowed?
Why do mathematicians need an agreed order at all?
What is the reciprocal of 5, and what do you get when you multiply 5 by it?

topic.name: Sign Rules for Multiplication
topic.description: Multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the rules for the sign of the product or quotient
evidence: Apply the sign rules when multiplying two integers (positive × negative, negative × negative)
Apply the sign rules when dividing two integers
Solve multi-step real-world problems involving all four operations with positive and negative rational numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that a negative times a negative makes a positive, can they use that rule to work out calculations like '−3 × −4 = 12' — and explain why it makes sense?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–13: multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the RULES for the sign of a product or quotient (−×− = +, −×+ = −, and the same for ÷).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): pupils 'use the four operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers... both positive and negative', and understand and use the rules of arithmetic with negative numbers.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 7.NS.2 — apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide rational numbers, understanding that the rules for signs come from requiring the distributive property to keep holding.
• Operational details — the sign of a product/quotient depends only on the signs of the factors: same signs → positive, different signs → negative; compute the magnitude as usual, then apply the sign. Crucially, DERIVE −×− = + rather than assert it: via patterns (−3×2, −3×1, −3×0, −3×−1 continuing the +3 step), via repeated-addition/'removing debts', and via the distributive law (−3×(2+−2) = 0). Extend to rationals and to multi-step real-world contexts (temperature, money, debts).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): apply the sign rule to a single product (−7×3 = −21, −4×−5 = 20). Tier B (11–13): apply sign rules to division and to products of rationals. Tier C (13): solve a multi-step real-world problem mixing all four operations with positive and negative rationals, tracking signs correctly.
bestPractices: DERIVE the two-negatives-make-a-positive rule instead of asserting it: extend a multiplication pattern (−3×2=−6, −3×1=−3, −3×0=0, −3×−1=+3, −3×−2=+6) so the +3 step forces the sign flip — rules learnt by pattern resist the 'why?' confusion.
Reinforce with a real context/model: −×− as 'removing debts' (taking away several −£5 debts increases your balance) or reversing direction twice on a number line, so the rule has meaning.

Separate MAGNITUDE from SIGN: compute the numbers as usual, then decide the sign by counting negatives — an even number of negatives gives positive, odd gives negative; extends cleanly to longer products.
Connect × and ÷ sign rules as one system (they share the rule) and to the inverse relationship, so division signs aren't relearned separately.
Distinguish sign-of-operation from sign-of-number early to pre-empt confusion with adding/subtracting negatives (the prerequisite), e.g. −5 − −3 vs −5 × −3.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication pattern table stepping through −3×2 down to −3×−2, exposing the constant +3 step that forces −×− = +.
Sign-only grid: rows/columns of + and − giving the product's sign, abstracted from magnitude.
Number-line 'direction reversal' model: multiplying by a negative flips direction; two negatives flip twice.
Debt/temperature context cards giving −×− concrete meaning (removing debts, temperature-change rates).
commonMisconceptions: −×− = −: assuming two negatives stay negative (over-generalising from addition where − + − is more negative).
Confusing the sign rules for ×÷ with those for +− (−5 + −3 vs −5 × −3).
Applying the sign but mis-computing magnitude, or vice versa — not separating the two decisions.
Sign errors in longer products — losing track of how many negatives (even vs odd) determines the result.
Thinking dividing by a negative behaves differently from multiplying by one, rather than following the same rule.

learn.summary: For ages 11–13: multiply and divide positive and negative integers and rational numbers, with the sign of a product or quotient understood through DERIVATION rather than assertion — especially why negative × negative = positive. Learners separate the magnitude computation from the sign decision, see × and ÷ as sharing one sign rule, and keep that rule out of additive steps. The signature activity is a 'sign lab' that steps a multiplication pattern until the +3 step forces the double-negative result, reinforced by a direction-reversal number-line model and real-world debt/temperature meaning. Alternatives — a sign/pattern reference grid, a Socratic debt-analogy dialogue, and fluency checks on the sign of products/quotients — are preserved with their distinct purposes and limits.

activities.title: Sign lab: derive why negative × negative = positive
feedback: If a learner writes −3×−1 = −3, replay the pattern: −6, −3, 0 rose by +3 each step, so the next line must be +3 — the minus cannot stay.
If they get the magnitude but guess the sign, prompt 'count the negatives first — even or odd?' and have them re-mark the answer before computing.
When the number-line arrow flips twice back to positive, name it: 'two reversals return you to the start — that is why two negatives give a positive.'
If a learner thinks division behaves differently, pair 20 ÷ −5 = −4 with 4 × −5 = −20: both have different-signed factors, so both results are negative — showing × and ÷ obey the same sign rule.
activities.rationale: Deriving the rule via a continued pattern (and connecting it to the distributive law and a debt model) is reported to be more robust than asserting it, which invites the −×− = − error. Separating sign from magnitude, counting negatives for longer products, and reusing one rule for × and ÷ target the specific misconceptions catalogued for this topic. A live pattern table, direction-reversing number-line arrow, and even/odd counter are offered as concrete ways to make the flip felt; they are illustrative, not mandatory.

learnerActions: Step down a multiplication pattern one line at a time: −3×2 = −6, −3×1 = −3, −3×0 = 0, −3×−1 = ?, −3×−2 = ? Hold the constant +3 step at each line, and say what the pattern forces the next answer to be before computing.
State out loud why −3×−1 must be +3 and −3×−2 must be +6, using the continued pattern as your justification.
On a number line, model multiplying by a negative as flipping an arrow's direction; multiply by two negatives and watch the arrow flip twice back to positive.

For a longer product such as (−2)×(−3)×(−1)×(−4), count the negatives (even or odd) to predict the sign first, then compute the magnitude 2×3×1×4 = 24 and attach the sign (four negatives → positive, so +24).
Switch to division (e.g. 20 ÷ −5 = −4, −48 ÷ −6 = +8) and check the same-signs→positive, different-signs→negative rule applies, deciding the sign before the magnitude.
activities.intendedInsight: For nonzero numbers, the sign of a product or quotient depends only on the signs of the numbers involved (same signs → positive, different signs → negative); a zero factor gives 0, and division by zero is undefined. −×− = + is forced by continuing the multiplication pattern (and by requiring the distributive property to keep holding), not merely asserted. Counting negatives (even → positive, odd → negative) extends the rule to longer products of nonzero factors, and division obeys the identical rule.

activities.title: Debt and temperature: real meaning for removing negatives
feedback: If a learner turns −12 − (−2) into −14, point out that subtracting a negative moves UP the line (+2), giving −10; the multiplication rule does not govern this step.
If they say −3 + −4 = +7, contrast it with −3 × −4 = +12: 'two negatives make a positive' is a MULTIPLY/DIVIDE rule; adding two negatives moves further down to −7.
Praise reasoning that states the sign and its meaning ('removing a debt adds to my balance'), not just the numerical answer.
activities.rationale: A real context gives −×− concrete meaning and supports extension to multi-step problems with rationals, matching the age-appropriate standards. Explicitly separating the sign-of-operation (+−) from the sign rule for ×÷ pre-empts the dominant interference error where learners over-generalise 'two negatives make a positive' to addition. The debt/temperature skins are illustrative supports, not the only valid context.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the four operations applied to positive and negative integers, and understand and use the rules of arithmetic with negative numbers.
Deriving −×− = + via a continued multiplication pattern (or the distributive law / debt model) is more robust than asserting the rule, which invites the −×− = − error.
learnerActions: Interpret −×− through removing repeated debts: if taking away one −£5 debt raises your balance by £5, work out what removing four −£5 debts does, and write it as (−4)×(−5) = +20.
Match a temperature-change context to a signed product (e.g. a rate of −3°C per hour, run backwards over −2 hours gives +6°C), and explain the sign in words.

Solve a short multi-step real-world problem mixing operations with positive and negative rationals, tracking the sign at each step, e.g. (−3)×4 − (−2): compute −12, then subtracting −2 means add 2, giving −10.
After the multi-step item, check whether you accidentally let the multiplication sign rule leak into the addition/subtraction step.
activities.intendedInsight: Signed multiplication and division carry real meaning (removing debts, reversing a rate over negative time), which anchors the sign rules; and the ×÷ 'two negatives make a positive' rule must NOT be applied to addition or subtraction, where adding a negative moves down the number line.

activities.title: Justify it aloud: a Socratic challenge (alternative)
feedback: If the justification is only 'the rule says so', ask them to walk the pattern −6, −3, 0 and continue it — a reason, not a recital.

If they extend the rule to addition, redirect to the number line: adding a negative moves down, so −3 + −4 lands at −7. In addition, the sign of the answer comes from where you land, not from a 'two negatives' sign rule.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue fits the derivation goal by demanding justification and surfacing the slogan-only response level described in the assessment. It is offered as a complement: spoken justification can check and build reasoning, while hands-on pattern/number-line manipulation makes the flip concrete. No claim is made that talk alone is sufficient or superior.
sourceClaims: Deriving −×− = + via a continued multiplication pattern (or the distributive law / debt model) is more robust than asserting the rule, which invites the −×− = − error.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge 'why does minus times minus give plus?' by justifying −3×−2 = +6 using either the continued pattern or a debt story, in your own words.
Defend your reasoning when pushed: 'couldn't it stay negative because there are negatives in it?' — explain why the pattern forbids that.
Explain, in the same conversation, why the rule does NOT make −3 + −4 positive.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate WHY −×− = + (not just state it) distinguishes genuine understanding from a recited slogan, and surfaces whether the learner wrongly extends the rule to addition.

activities.title: Sign reference grid and fluency check (scaffold + check)
feedback: When a learner selects −×− = −, replay the pattern derivation rather than just marking it wrong.
If signs are right on × but hesitant on ÷, pair the two to show one shared rule.
Reward deciding the sign before the magnitude, and re-marking any answer where the sign was an afterthought.
activities.rationale: Recognition and sorting tasks are efficient for checking fluency and can surface the −×− = − misconception with a targeted distractor, but by themselves they test the rule rather than elicit the derivation of why it holds — so they follow, not replace, the sign-lab work. A static grid is a useful anchor but cannot run the pattern dynamically, so it supplements rather than substitutes for the derivation.
learnerActions: Use a +/− product grid (rows and columns of signs) to read off the sign of a product abstracted from magnitude; reveal a worked example for each cell.
Decide the sign of a mixed set quickly: −4×−5, −20÷4, a rational product, sorting each into positive or negative.
Spot and explain the classic trap −×− = − when it appears as a tempting wrong answer.
Match multiplication and division pairs that share the same sign rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Once derived, the sign rule can be applied fluently and consistently across multiplication and division; a sign-only grid abstracts the rule from magnitude, and quick checks build and confirm fluency.

constraints: The central objective is DERIVING the sign rules (especially −×− = +), not asserting them; any activity should let the learner reach the double-negative result by pattern, direction-reversal, distributive reasoning, or debt model before stating it.

Recognition/sorting/matching tasks (grid, multiple-choice, categorisation) check fluency and can surface the −×− = − error but do not by themselves show the learner WHY the rule holds; keep them downstream of the derivation.
A static sign/pattern grid is an anchor and reference; it cannot step the pattern live or show the arrow reversing, so treat it as a scaffold, not the derivation itself.

Always separate the sign-of-operation (+ and −) from the sign rule for × and ÷: do not let 'two negatives make a positive' leak into addition/subtraction. Re-anchor additive moves on the number line as a prerequisite.

Keep the magnitude decision and the sign decision distinct: compute the numbers as usual, decide the sign by counting negatives (even → positive, odd → negative), provided no factor is zero (any zero factor makes the product 0, and division by zero is undefined).

Interactive examples (live pattern table, flipping number-line vector, even/odd counter, debt/temperature skin, tap-to-reveal grid cells) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are optional, not mandatory, and the same learning can be done with paper and spoken reasoning.
A full 3D environment is not needed; at most a 1D direction model is relevant here. This is a scoping note, not a claim that other media cannot teach the rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the three cited sources were NOT re-fetched and all carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: pattern −3×2=−6, −3×1=−3, −3×0=0, −3×−1=+3, −3×−2=+6 is correct (+3 step). Checks −7×3=−21, −4×−5=20, −7×−3=+21, 20÷−5=−4, −48÷−6=+8, (−2)×(−3)×(−1)×(−4)=+24 are correct. Multi-step (−3)×4 − (−2) = −12 + 2 = −10 is correct; the interference errors (−14, +14, +10 with wrong sign) are deliberately wrong learner outputs kept only as diagnostic signals, never as endorsed answers or learner-facing options.
Corrected a duplicated-word clarity defect in activity[0] action 5 ('same same-signs' → 'same-signs'); no factual change.

Candidate feedback originally paired '−20÷4 with −4×5 (both give −20/−4 territory)', which was garbled and could imply the two expressions are equal; corrected to 20÷−5 = −4 vs 4×−5 = −20, equal only in sign, to demonstrate that × and ÷ share one sign rule.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Using inverse operations
topic.description: Recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations; use these relationships to check answers and simplify calculations
evidence: Use addition and subtraction as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Use multiplication and division as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Recognise that squaring and square-rooting are inverse operations
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out '252 ÷ 7 = 36', can they immediately use the inverse to check — '36 × 7 = 252' — without having to redo the division?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: recognise and USE relationships between operations, especially INVERSE operations (+/−, ×/÷, squaring/square-rooting), to check answers and simplify calculations — the formal foundation for solving and rearranging equations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'recognise and use relationships between operations, including inverse operations' and use inverse operations/estimation to check calculations.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on the inverse relationship of ×÷ (3.OA.6, unknown-factor division) and of +−, extended toward 6.EE.5–7 (solving one-step equations by inverse) and squaring/rooting (8.EE.2).
• Operational details — make explicit that each operation is UNDONE by its inverse: add↔subtract, multiply↔divide, square↔square-root. Use this two ways: (i) CHECK a result (compute 156÷12 = 13, verify 13×12 = 156), and (ii) SOLVE for an unknown by applying the inverse to isolate it (□ + 7 = 20 → □ = 20 − 7). Emphasise 'doing the same to both sides' and the balance/equation model. This is the bridge to linear equations (dependent mt_QhFEDyIwSO) and rearranging formulae (mt_3qrCtdoVAU).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): use ×÷ as inverses to check a calculation. Tier B (11–12): solve a one-step unknown by applying the inverse and justify it. Tier C (12): recognise squaring and square-rooting as inverses and use inverse operations to check a multi-step result.
bestPractices: Make CHECKING routine: after any calculation, undo it with the inverse (13×12 to check 156÷12) — embedding inverse relationships as a self-verification habit, connecting to estimation-checking.

Use the BALANCE / equation model — whatever you do to one side you do to the other — so applying an inverse is seen as keeping equality, not a trick; build from fact families and bar models already secured.

Teach inverse operations in ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS reverse when unpicking multi-step expressions (undo +/− outer layer, then ×÷), foreshadowing equation rearrangement — the prerequisite BODMAS understanding (mt_jHgRQ4hR0g) is exactly why the undo order matters.
Include squaring↔square-rooting as an inverse pair, noting the ± subtlety (√ of a square recovers the magnitude), to broaden 'inverse' beyond the four basic operations.
Use empty-box and function-machine tasks (input→×3→+2→output; run backwards to find the input) so inverse becomes 'run the machine in reverse'.
keyRepresentations: Function machine run forwards and BACKWARDS, each step replaced by its inverse in reverse order.
Balance-scale / equation model showing the same inverse applied to both sides to isolate the unknown.
Fact-family triangle (a, b, a×b) linking a multiplication to its two divisions — inverse made concrete.
Inverse-pair chart: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷, square ↔ √.
commonMisconceptions: Undoing operations in the WRONG order (undoing the × before the + in a two-step machine) — not reversing the order of operations.
Applying the inverse to only one side of an equation, breaking the balance.
Confusing inverse (undo) with commutative/associative relationships, or thinking subtraction 'undoes' multiplication.
Believing squaring and square-rooting are perfect inverses without the ± / non-negative subtlety.
Treating 'inverse' as merely reversing the numbers (12÷156 to check 156÷12) rather than applying the inverse operation.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, teach inverse operations (add↔subtract, multiply↔divide by a non-zero number, square↔square-root for non-negative numbers) as a way to UNDO calculations — both to check results and to solve for an unknown by isolating it. Core principles: undoing a multi-step process reverses both the operations AND their order (last done, first undone); and 'do the same to both sides' keeps an equation balanced. This is the concrete foundation for solving and rearranging equations. Build the do/undo intuition through function-machine and balance-scale work, then consolidate and probe reasoning.

activities.title: Function machine: run it forwards, then run it backwards
feedback: If a learner reverses the operations but keeps the forward order, have them compare the two attempts numerically: only 'undo +2, then ÷3' returns the start value. Rehearse with a second two-step example.
If they only swap the numbers (e.g. 12÷156 to 'check' 156÷12), point out that an inverse changes the OPERATION, not just the order of the numbers.
Reinforce with a fact-family triangle (a, b, a×b) so the undo is concrete: one multiplication and its two divisions live in the same triangle.
activities.rationale: Running a function machine forwards and then backwards makes 'undo in reverse order' a felt consequence rather than a stated rule, directly confronting the common error of reversing operations without reversing their order.
sourceClaims: The balance/equation model and function machines run in reverse make inverse operations and 'do the same to both sides' explicit, bridging to solving and rearranging equations.
learnerActions: Build a two-step machine, e.g. '×3 then +2'. Drop in an input (say 5) and record the output (17).
Now recover the original input WITHOUT being told it: work out which operation to undo first and which second. (Undo +2 first → 15, then ÷3 → 5.)
Deliberately try undoing in the forward order instead (÷3 first, then −2) and check whether you get back the start number. Notice it does NOT return 5 — this shows why the order must reverse.
State the rule in your own words: to undo a chain, reverse both the operations and their order (last done is first undone).

If a live model is available, flip the machine into REVERSE mode so each step is automatically swapped for its inverse and reordered, and compare it with a manual attempt that undoes the steps in the forward order; that wrong-order attempt visibly fails to return the starting value.
activities.intendedInsight: Each operation is undone by its inverse, and to undo a sequence you must reverse BOTH the operations and their order.

activities.title: Balance scale: solving one-step unknowns by keeping both sides equal
feedback: If a learner changes only one side, use the tilting balance (or draw the scale tipping) to show equality is broken; redo applying the inverse to both sides.
If they pick the wrong inverse (e.g. add 7 to solve □ + 7 = 20), ask what operation currently acts on □ and what undoes it.
Connect to fact families and bar models already secured so the move feels familiar.
activities.rationale: The balance model represents applying an inverse as maintaining equality, addressing the misconception of operating on only one side and building the bridge to formal equation solving.
sourceClaims: Division is defined as an unknown-factor problem (the inverse of multiplication), and one-step equations are solved by applying inverse operations while maintaining equality.
The balance/equation model and function machines run in reverse make inverse operations and 'do the same to both sides' explicit, bridging to solving and rearranging equations.
learnerActions: Look at a balance representing □ + 7 = 20. Decide which inverse isolates the unknown (subtract 7).
Apply that inverse to BOTH sides and read off □ = 20 − 7 = 13.
Try applying the inverse to only one side and predict what happens to the balance — it tilts, because the two sides are no longer equal.
Repeat with a multiplication case, e.g. 3·□ = 21 (divide both sides by 3 → □ = 7).
Explain why 'do the same to both sides' keeps the statement true.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying an inverse isolates the unknown, and doing it to both sides preserves equality — it is not a trick but a consequence of keeping the balance level.

activities.title: Checking a calculation by undoing it
feedback: If a learner checks by redoing the same operation, show that the same error (especially a method error) is likely to reappear; the inverse (×) tests the result more independently.

If they invert incorrectly — for example repeating the same division, or multiplying an unrelated/wrong pair such as 156 × 12 instead of computing the correct 13 × 12 — build the fact-family triangle for the three numbers so the correct check is visible. (Note: dividing the dividend by the quotient, 156 ÷ 13 = 12, is actually a valid alternative check, so do not treat it as an error.)
For squaring/rooting, note the ± / non-negative subtlety so learners do not treat them as perfectly symmetric inverses.
activities.rationale: Embedding inverse-checking as a self-verification routine consolidates the relationship and connects to estimation-checking, while addressing the error of 'checking' by repeating the same operation.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations, and use inverse operations and estimation to check calculations.
learnerActions: Compute a division such as 156 ÷ 12 = 13.
Check it by applying the inverse: 13 × 12. Confirm it returns exactly 156.

Discuss why re-dividing (156 ÷ 12 again) is a weaker check: repeating the same operation tends to repeat the same mistake (especially a mistake in method), whereas the inverse is a more independent check.
Try a square/root pair: check √49 = 7 by squaring (7² = 49). Note the subtlety that √ of a square recovers the non-negative magnitude.
Make checking a habit: after any calculation, undo it with its inverse.
activities.intendedInsight: Inverse operations provide an independent verification of a result; redoing the same operation does not.

activities.title: Talk it through: how would you check that, and which inverse isolates it?
feedback: If the learner only says 'do the division again', prompt: what operation would UNDO the division? Steer toward multiplication and have them explain why it is independent.
If they reverse a two-step calculation but keep the order, rehearse 'last done, first undone' with the ×3-then-+4 example.
Listen for the reason, not just the right calculation: a strong response names multiplication and division as inverses that undo each other.
activities.rationale: A relational idea like inverse operations is well probed by questioning that elicits the learner's reasoning about undoing, including reversing the order of steps, surfacing whether a learner checks by inverse or merely by repeating; questioning may elicit this reasoning but does not by itself guarantee it.
learnerActions: A child worked out 138 ÷ 6 = 23. Without redoing the division, say what single calculation would CHECK whether 23 is right, and explain why that check works.
Answer and justify: multiply 23 × 6; if it returns 138 the answer is right, because multiplication undoes division.
Respond to the probe: 'Someone checked 138 ÷ 6 by dividing again and got 23 — does that prove it is right?' Explain why repeating the same operation is not an independent check.
Tackle a two-step undo: 'If I did ×3 then +4 to a number, how would you get back to the start?' (Undo +4 first, then ÷3.)
Consider squaring/rooting: how would you check √49 = 7?
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the inverse relationship — naming the OPPOSITE operation and why undoing works — distinguishes genuine understanding from merely re-running a procedure.

activities.title: Consolidation: match, sequence and solve
feedback: Matching and sequencing confirm recall but do not by themselves build the do/undo intuition — pair them with at least one 'explain why' prompt so reasoning is exercised, not only recognition.
If undo order is sequenced wrongly, send the learner back to a function machine to test the sequence numerically.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks are efficient for consolidation once the do/undo intuition is built; they test rather than construct it, so they follow the hands-on and dialogic activities.
learnerActions: Match each operation to its inverse: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷ (by a non-zero number), square ↔ √ (for non-negative numbers).
Given a two-step machine, put the undo steps in the correct reverse order.
Fill in the solving step for one-step unknowns, e.g. □ + 7 = 20 → □ = 20 − 7.
Explain, for at least one item, WHY the chosen inverse is correct, not just which it is.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of inverse pairs and correct reverse-order undoing supports later equation work.

constraints: Matching, sequencing and fill-in-the-blank tasks assess recall and recognition; they do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a check or the felt experience of reversing order, so they are best used to consolidate rather than introduce the idea.

A static labelled diagram of a function machine or balance can serve as a reference, but it cannot let the learner run the chain backwards or see the balance tilt when only one side is changed; those consequences are what make the rule stick.
Treat squaring and square-rooting as inverses WITH the non-negative/± subtlety: √ of a square returns the magnitude. Do not present them as perfectly symmetric inverses.
To undo a multi-step calculation, reverse both the operations AND their order; reversing operations while keeping the forward order is a common and specific error to confront directly.
An inverse changes the operation, not merely the order of the numbers (12 ÷ 156 is not the inverse check of 156 ÷ 12).

A valid inverse check of 156 ÷ 12 = 13 can be either 13 × 12 = 156 or 156 ÷ 13 = 12; both independently recover a known quantity. The genuine error is repeating the same division or multiplying an unrelated pair.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 5→×3→15→+2→17, and undoing 17→−2→15→÷3→5 is correct; undoing in forward order (17÷3≈5.67, then −2) does not return 5, confirming order must reverse. 156 ÷ 12 = 13 and 13 × 12 = 156 check out. 138 ÷ 6 = 23 and 23 × 6 = 138 are correct. 3·□ = 21 → □ = 7 is correct. √49 = 7 and 7² = 49 are correct.

The original assessment probe asks 'Why does multiplying 23 by 6 check the division' — correct, since 23 × 6 = 138. A source distractor listed '138 × 6' (=828) as a wrong check, which is genuinely wrong and is retained only as an error pattern, never as a valid check.

The original assessment error pattern lists 'divides 138 by 23' (and an analogous '156 ÷ 13') as a wrong inverse. This is a questionable original example: dividing the dividend by the quotient recovers the divisor and is in fact a valid independent check. The corrected feedback uses genuinely wrong moves (repeating the same division, or multiplying an unrelated/wrong pair) instead, and this is noted in the activity feedback itself, not only here.

Activity 4 (dialogic probing) carries no sourceClaim: the available claims support function-machine/balance representations, not the efficacy of Socratic questioning, so [] is used. Efficacy of the questioning approach is proposed, not established.

The balance model is a representation of equality maintenance; it is offered as an effective scaffold, not as the only possible way to teach inverse operations. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the available sources.

Squaring and square-rooting — are those inverses too? How would you check √49 = 7?

It works because multiplication and division are inverse operations — multiplying the quotient by the divisor undoes the division and must return the original number. A child reasoning well names the inverse relationship, not just 'do it again'.

topic.name: Decimal place value
topic.description: Multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers (e.g. 3.47 × 6)
evidence: Correctly compute 4.56 × 7 using a written method
Use place-value reasoning to explain why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0
Model a decimal multiplication using an area diagram or expanded form
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '3.47 × 6' — keeping the decimal point in the right place and carrying correctly through each column?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: multiply numbers with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6), using place-value reasoning and a written method, understanding the answer's decimal places.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.7 — multiply decimals to hundredths using concrete models/drawings and strategies based on place value; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning.
• Operational details — the powerful approach is 'multiply as whole numbers, then scale back by the powers of ten you removed': treat 3.47 as 347 hundredths, compute 347×6 = 2082, then ÷100 to get 20.82. Support with the area model (partition 3.47 into 3 + 0.4 + 0.07, multiply each by 6, recombine) and with estimation (3.47×6 ≈ 3.5×6 = 21) to place the point. Emphasise WHY the answer has the decimal places it does, not a 'count the decimal places' rule applied blindly.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute 3.2×5 and explain via place value why it is 16.0. Tier B (10–11): compute 4.56×7 with a written method and a matching estimate. Tier C (11): model 3.47×6 with an area diagram or expanded form and justify the placement of the decimal point.
bestPractices: Teach 'compute as whole numbers, then rescale by the powers of ten': 3.47 = 347 ÷ 100, so 3.47×6 = (347×6) ÷ 100 — connecting to the ×÷-by-powers-of-ten work (mt_wPgpMJ0-PA) and giving a reason for the decimal placement.
Always pair the calculation with an ESTIMATE (3.47×6 ≈ 21) so the decimal point is placed by sense, not by a mechanical digit-count that fails learners when trailing zeros vanish.

Use the area model / expanded form: partition the decimal into whole, tenths and hundredths, multiply each part by the whole number, and sum — making the distributive structure and each place's contribution visible.

Confront the 'line up the decimal points' import from addition: it does NOT apply to this multiplication — the answer's places come from the scaling, and children should predict then check with an estimate.
Address trailing zeros explicitly (3.2×5 = 16.0 = 16): the 'count decimal places' rule seems to give 16.0, and children must understand equivalence rather than think a place has been lost.
keyRepresentations: Area model / grid: rows for 3, 0.4, 0.07 (or expanded 3.47) × the whole number, each cell a partial product to be summed.
'Scale out, scale back' chain: 3.47 → ×100 → 347 → ×6 → 2082 → ÷100 → 20.82, linking to powers-of-ten shifting.
Place-value columns showing the partial products aligned by place (ones, tenths, hundredths).
Estimate bracket: 3.47×6 sitting between 3×6 = 18 and 4×6 = 24, anchoring the point at 20.82.
commonMisconceptions: Blindly 'counting decimal places' without understanding, then mishandling trailing zeros (3.2×5 → thinking 16.0 is wrong, or 1.60).
Importing 'line up the decimal points' from decimal addition into multiplication.
Multiplying only the whole-number part or only one place (3.47×6 done as 3×6 = 18).
Misplacing the decimal point (2.082 or 208.2) because the point was not reasoned via scaling or estimate.
Forgetting to rescale after computing the whole-number product (leaving 2082 instead of 20.82).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: multiply numbers with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6) by computing as whole numbers and rescaling by the powers of ten removed, supported by the area/expanded model and estimation to place the decimal point by reasoning rather than a rote 'count the decimal places' rule.

activities.title: Decimal area builder: partition, multiply, recombine
feedback: If the learner only computes 3 × 6 = 18 (or 4 × 7 = 28), point out that the tenths and hundredths parts still have to be multiplied and added in — ask what 0.4 × 6 and 0.07 × 6 contribute.
If the partial products are right but the sum is wrong, have them re-add aligning ones with ones, tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.
Confirm 20.82 and 31.92 by checking each coloured partial product lines up in the correct place column.
activities.rationale: An area/expanded-form partition makes the distributive contribution of each place visible and directly counters the error of multiplying only the whole-number part. A live or hands-on build where partial products recombine can make the recombination concrete, though a static coloured grid can also anchor the same structure.
sourceClaims: Pupils multiply decimals to hundredths using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
learnerActions: Break 3.47 into place-value parts: 3, 0.4 and 0.07.
Multiply each part by 6 and record the partial products: 3 × 6 = 18, 0.4 × 6 = 2.4, 0.07 × 6 = 0.42.
Add the partial products to recombine: 18 + 2.4 + 0.42 = 20.82.
Shade or colour each partial product by its place (ones, tenths, hundredths) so each place's contribution to the total is visible.
Repeat independently for 4.56 × 7: partition into 4, 0.5, 0.06; multiply each by 7 (28, 3.5, 0.42); sum to 31.92.
activities.intendedInsight: Every part of the decimal multiplies by the whole number, and the total is the sum of the partial products — the distributive structure, not just a digit the child forgot.

activities.title: Scale out, scale back
feedback: If the learner leaves the answer as 2082 or 3192, ask what scaling they still owe — they multiplied by 100 at the start and must divide by 100 to finish.
If they place the point as 2.082 or 208.2, walk back through the ÷100 step: 2082 ÷ 100 shifts two places to give 20.82.
Link this to earlier work on multiplying and dividing by powers of ten — the same place-value shift is happening here.
activities.rationale: Treating the decimal as a whole number and rescaling connects decimal multiplication to powers-of-ten reasoning and gives a justified basis for decimal placement. This supports learners who misapply or get confused by a 'count the places' rule, for example with trailing zeros (writing 160 as 16 first and then counting one place to get 1.6, or worrying that 16.0 = 16 has 'lost' a place).
sourceClaims: Estimating the product first, and reasoning via place-value scaling, places the decimal point more reliably than a mechanical 'count the decimal places' rule.
learnerActions: Scale 3.47 up by ×100 to the friendly whole number 347.
Multiply: 347 × 6 = 2082.
Scale back down by ÷100 to recover 20.82.
Explain in your own words why the ÷100 is needed: you removed a factor of 100 at the start, so you must put it back.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal places in the answer come from the scaling you did (and undid), giving a reason for the decimal point's position rather than a memorised count.

activities.title: Estimate first, place the point by sense
feedback: If the learner gives 3.192 or 319.2, ask how big the answer should be: since 4.56 × 7 ≈ 32, only 31.92 fits.
If they cannot estimate, prompt them to round 4.56 to 4.5 (or to 5) and multiply that by 7.
Praise placing the point by comparing to the estimate rather than by counting digits alone.
activities.rationale: Pairing every calculation with an estimate makes decimal placement a reasoned act and provides a self-check. An out-of-range flag (e.g. an estimate bracket the answer must sit within) makes the magnitude check concrete.
sourceClaims: Estimating the product first, and reasoning via place-value scaling, places the decimal point more reliably than a mechanical 'count the decimal places' rule.
learnerActions: Before computing 4.56 × 7, estimate: 4.56 ≈ 4.5, so 4.56 × 7 ≈ 4.5 × 7 = 31.5, i.e. about 32 (bracket it between 4 × 7 = 28 and 5 × 7 = 35).
Compute the whole-number product and place the decimal point so the answer is close to your estimate (about 32), giving 31.92.
Test the wrong placements: check whether 3.192 or 319.2 is anywhere near 32 — they are not, so they must be wrong.
State out loud how your estimate told you where the point belongs.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate of the product's size tells you where the decimal point must go, catching off-by-a-power-of-ten mistakes that a rote count would miss.

activities.title: Trailing zeros: why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0 = 16
feedback: If the learner worries a decimal place disappeared, show 16.0 and 16 mark the same point on a number line.
If they offer 1.60, ask whether 3.2 × 5 should be about 15 or about 1.6 — the estimate settles it.
Reinforce that equivalence (16.0 = 16), not a lost digit, explains the tidy whole-number answer.
activities.rationale: Trailing zeros are a known stumbling block when a mechanical count rule is applied; making the equivalence explicit and checking with an estimate defuses the 'I lost a decimal place' worry.
learnerActions: Compute 3.2 × 5: multiply 32 × 5 = 160, then rescale ÷10 to get 16.0.
Explain why 16.0 and 16 are the same number — the trailing zero after the decimal point adds no value.
Discuss why a blind 'count one decimal place in, so one decimal place out' seems to demand 16.0 but does not mean a place was 'lost'.
Contrast with the wrong answer 1.60: use an estimate (3.2 × 5 ≈ 15) to show 1.60 is far too small.
activities.intendedInsight: A result like 16.0 simplifies to 16 by equivalence; no place is lost, and an estimate confirms the true size.

activities.title: Don't line up decimal points as in addition
feedback: If the learner keeps the point aligned through the multiplication and muddles the digits, have them redo it ignoring the point, then replace it using the estimate.
Name the habit explicitly: 'point alignment belongs to adding and subtracting, not to this multiplication.'
Confirm the final placement against the estimate (≈32 for 4.56 × 7).
activities.rationale: Importing point-alignment from addition is a documented misconception; explicitly separating the two procedures and placing the point last prevents it.
learnerActions: Set out 4.56 × 7 by multiplying as if the number were whole (456 × 7), ignoring the point during the multiplication.
Place the decimal point only at the end, using the scaling or estimate.
Compare this with decimal addition, where points ARE aligned, and state why the two procedures differ.
Catch the muddle: try to 'keep the point aligned' through the multiplication and notice how the digits become confused.
activities.intendedInsight: Lining up decimal points is an addition habit; in this multiplication the point is placed at the end from the scaling, not kept aligned during the digit work.

constraints: This objective is multiplying a number with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6, 4.56 × 7); it is not multiplying two decimals together.
Learners must be able to justify decimal placement via place-value scaling or estimation, not merely recite a 'count the decimal places' rule they cannot explain.
Address trailing zeros explicitly: 3.2 × 5 = 16.0 = 16; ensure learners understand the equivalence rather than fearing a lost place.

A pre-built, tap-to-reveal worked model can anchor the method but does not let learners vary the numbers or perform the recombination themselves; use it as a reference alongside tasks where learners build and compute.

Multiple-choice point-placement items (e.g. choosing between 208.2 / 20.82 / 2.082) and fill-the-blank partial products test the outcome and are useful for practice, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the method or the reasoning behind placement.

For this planar place-value/area concept, a 2D area model is sufficient and a genuine third spatial dimension offers no clear additional affordance over it; 3D representation is not required here. This is a scoped observation about this topic, not a universal rule that 3D adds nothing in general.
Prerequisite: multiplying and dividing by powers of ten (the scale-out/scale-back move depends on it).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the US standard 5.NBT.7 claim and the NCETM claim as unverified (verified:false); only the DfE Year 6 claim is marked verified. Treat the estimation-reliability claim as guidance, not established comparative efficacy.

The pedagogy frames the whole-number-then-rescale method as 'the powerful approach'; this is a reasonable, standards-aligned strategy but is presented without comparative evidence of superiority over other valid written methods.

The original research ranked a 3D interactive as 'poor' with the categorical claim that 3D 'adds nothing'; this has been rewritten as a scoped, qualified limitation about this planar topic rather than a universal law.

topic.name: Division with Decimals
topic.description: Use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places; divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers
evidence: Compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method to get 3.69
Explain how to continue long division past the decimal point to obtain a decimal quotient
Solve a context problem that requires dividing a decimal amount equally (e.g. sharing £18.60 among 5 people)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a written method to calculate something like '17 ÷ 4 = 4.25' — carrying the division past the decimal point to get a decimal answer rather than a remainder?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: use written division where the answer has up to two decimal places — divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers (e.g. 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69), and continue division past the decimal point.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.7 — divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies, models, and relating to a written method; 6.NS.3 fluency with decimal division.
• Operational details — the key move is continuing short/long division past the decimal point, carrying the remainder to the next place: 14.76 ÷ 4 proceeds 14÷4 = 3 r2, bring down 7 (as 27 tenths), 27÷4 = 6 r3, bring down 6 (36 hundredths), 36÷4 = 9 → 3.69, keeping the point aligned. Where a whole number doesn't divide exactly, annex zeros after the point (18.6 → 18.60) to continue. Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money/measures.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69 keeping the point aligned. Tier B (10–11): explain how to continue past the decimal point / annex a zero when a place won't divide. Tier C (11): solve a context problem needing decimal division (share £18.60 among 5) and interpret the answer as money.
bestPractices: Teach the decimal point in the quotient as ALIGNED with the point in the dividend — place it first, then divide place by place — so the point's position is structural, not an afterthought.

Show that continuing past the point is the SAME process as whole-number division: the remainder is regrouped into the next-smaller place (tenths, then hundredths), which children already know from long division of whole numbers (mt_WsM4EmdOLe).
Use annexing zeros deliberately: when there is a remainder at the last given place, adding a zero (13 ÷ 4 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue — grounded in equivalence, not a trick.
Anchor in context and estimation: sharing money/measures makes decimal quotients meaningful, and an estimate (14.76÷4 ≈ 15÷4 ≈ 3.7) sanity-checks the point placement.
Connect to ×÷ by powers of ten and place value (mt_wPgpMJ0-PA): dividing regroups a unit into ten of the next-smaller unit, exactly the place-value structure underpinning the method.
keyRepresentations: Short/long division layout (bus stop) with the quotient's decimal point drawn directly above the dividend's point before dividing.
Place-value regrouping picture: a leftover one 'exchanged' into ten tenths, a leftover tenth into ten hundredths, mirroring the carry.
Money/measure context model (£18.60 shared into 5 equal parts) that names the tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p.
Annexing-zeros illustration: 13 = 13.00 shown as equivalent, enabling the division to continue to 3.25.
commonMisconceptions: Misplacing or omitting the decimal point in the quotient (getting 369 or 36.9 for 14.76÷4).
Stopping at a remainder instead of continuing past the point or annexing a zero (13÷4 = 3 r1 left unfinished rather than 3.25).
Treating the tenths/hundredths digits as separate whole-number divisions without carrying the remainder down.
Writing the remainder as a whole number when the context calls for a decimal (money answer given as '3 remainder 2').
Losing place-value alignment so digits drift into the wrong column.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers using written division, continuing past the decimal point. The central insight is that the quotient's decimal point sits directly above the dividend's point (structural, not guessed), and that continuing past the point is the SAME regrouping used in whole-number division — each leftover is exchanged into ten of the next-smaller place. Worked anchor: 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69; and annexing zeros (13 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue when a remainder is left after the dividend's last digit (a place where the divisor doesn't fit instead gets a 0 in the quotient). Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5 = £3.72) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money and measures.

activities.title: Step-by-step divider: walk 14.76 ÷ 4
feedback: If the answer comes out as 369 or 36.9, the point was misplaced — line the quotient's point directly above the dividend's point and check the magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 is about 15 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is sensible.
If a leftover is dropped instead of exchanged, show the counters: 2 leftover ones become 20 tenths and join the next column before dividing again.
Verify the result by multiplying back: 3.69 × 4 = 14.76.
activities.rationale: Decimal division is a step-by-step regrouping procedure whose critical insight is point alignment; animating each remainder being exchanged into ten of the next-smaller unit and locking the quotient point above the dividend point makes both the process and its place-value structure felt. Optional supports — counters that visibly exchange one unit into ten of the next, and an estimate strip that flags a mis-placed point — make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
learnerActions: Before finding any digit, place the quotient's decimal point directly above the point in 14.76 — establish that its position is fixed by the dividend, not guessed.
Work left to right: 14 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 2. Show the leftover 2 ones being EXCHANGED into 20 tenths, which join the 7 tenths to make 27 tenths.
Continue: 27 tenths ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 3. Exchange the leftover 3 tenths into 30 hundredths, joining the 6 hundredths to make 36 hundredths.
Finish: 36 hundredths ÷ 4 = 9, giving 3.69 with the point aligned.
Narrate at each step: continuing 'past the decimal point' is the same regrouping already used for whole numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal point in the quotient is aligned structurally with the dividend's point, and dividing past the point is the familiar regrouping of a leftover into ten of the next-smaller place.

activities.title: Annex a zero to continue the division
feedback: If the child stops at '3 r1', remind them the leftover can be shared further: extend the dividend with a zero and keep dividing past the point.
If a decimal place is skipped when the divisor doesn't fit, insist that every brought-down decimal digit yields a quotient digit — write a 0 in the quotient for that place rather than omitting it.
Check 3.25 × 4 = 13 to confirm.
activities.rationale: Annexing zeros deliberately — grounded in equivalence rather than as a memorised rule — resolves the common error of stopping at a whole-number remainder, and reinforces that the written method continues place by place.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
learnerActions: Try 13 ÷ 4 and reach 3 remainder 1; notice the division is not finished.
Rewrite 13 as 13.00 (an equivalent value) and place the quotient point above it.
Continue dividing: carry the remainder 1 as 10 tenths, 10 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 2, carry 2 as 20 hundredths, 20 ÷ 4 = 5, giving 3.25.
Conclude that there was no real remainder — just more decimal places to find.
Repeat with 18.6 ÷ 5: annex a zero (18.60), continue to 3.72.
activities.intendedInsight: Annexing zeros after the decimal point is grounded in equivalence (13 = 13.00), not a trick; it lets division continue until it terminates or reaches the required number of places.

activities.title: Money and measures context: £18.60 shared among 5
feedback: If the answer is given as '3 remainder 3', ask what happens to the leftover money — it is shared further into 10p and 1p coins, so the division continues.
Estimate first: £18.60 ÷ 5 is about £20 ÷ 5 = £4, so £3.72 is sensible; an answer like £37.2 or £0.372 should be questioned by sense.
Confirm by multiplying back: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.rationale: Context and estimation anchor decimal quotients and make the point placement checkable by sense; naming tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p coins connects the abstract regrouping to money.
sourceClaims: Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
learnerActions: Set up £18.60 ÷ 5 as a written division, aligning the quotient point above the point in 18.60.

Divide: 18 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 3; exchange 3 leftover pounds into tenths (as 10p coins) with the 6 to make 36 tenths; 36 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 1; exchange into hundredths (1p coins) with the 0 to make 10 hundredths; 10 ÷ 5 = 2, giving £3.72.
Name the tenths as 10p coins and the hundredths as 1p coins so the regrouping is meaningful.
Interpret the answer as money: each person gets £3.72.
Check with multiplication: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal quotients are meaningful in context: sharing money or measures requires continuing past the point, and the answer must be interpreted (e.g. as pounds and pence), not left as a whole-number remainder.

activities.title: Place-the-point and finish-the-division practice
feedback: For the point-placement choice, reason from magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is right and 369 or 36.9 are off by powers of ten.
If the ordering omits annexing a zero where a remainder persists, point back to the equivalence 13 = 13.00.
These checks test the result; still ask the child to carry out an unaided written division to show the regrouping is understood, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items give efficient practice and expose the signature point-placement error, but they check results more than they build the regrouping procedure, so they supplement rather than replace independent written working.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing quotient digits for a partly-worked 14.76 ÷ 4.
Decide where the decimal point belongs, choosing between answers like 369, 36.9 and 3.69, and justify the choice by magnitude.
Put a set of division steps in order, including the step of annexing a zero to continue.
Match each quotient to the context problem it answers (e.g. a money-sharing problem).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a correct point placement and ordering the steps consolidates the procedure; estimation justifies the choice rather than guesswork.

activities.title: Talk it through: the leftover money problem
feedback: If the child says 'there's a remainder and we stop', prompt: can the £2 be shared as coins? Lead them to tenths (10p) and hundredths (1p).
Follow the discussion with written working so the verbal idea is grounded in the actual procedure.
activities.rationale: A spoken prompt about a leftover can probe whether the child sees that division continues past the point, but the procedural walk is better carried out through written working and manipulation, so this is a lead-in, not the main teaching.
learnerActions: Consider a scenario: money is shared equally but there is £2 left over — what now?
Explain aloud how to divide the leftover further into smaller coins (tenths and hundredths).
State where the decimal point goes in the answer and why.
Then carry out the full written division to confirm the spoken reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating what to do with a leftover surfaces the idea of continuing past the decimal point before formalising it in symbols.

constraints: The learning objective is carrying out written division past the decimal point: learners must produce the quotient digit by digit with correct point alignment, not merely recognise a correct answer.
Recognition and ordering tasks check results and expose point-placement errors, but they do not elicit independent construction of the regrouping procedure; pair them with unaided written division.
Tap-to-reveal worked examples are a reference model only — they do not let the child drive the division or annex zeros themselves, so follow them with learner-driven working.

Prerequisite links: regrouping a unit into ten of the next-smaller place draws on long division of whole numbers and on ×÷ by powers of ten / place value; reteach these if the point drifts or leftovers are dropped.
